questions.question: A physics teacher takes the turntable out of a microwave oven, lays a flat bar of chocolate inside and runs the oven for a few seconds. Melted spots appear about 6 centimetres apart. Each gap is half a wavelength, so each wave is about 12 centimetres long. The label on the back gives the oven's frequency as 2,450 million waves a second. What does she find by multiplying those two numbers?
choices: The speed of the microwaves
The energy of each microwave
The power of the oven
The heat in the chocolate
questions.context: Wave speed is frequency times wavelength: 2,450 million waves a second, each 0.12 metres long, make about 294 million metres a second, close to the 300 million metres a second at which light and every other electromagnetic wave crosses empty space. Real ovens heat unevenly, so the spots are not perfectly spaced and the result is only rough; measuring several gaps and averaging helps.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade physical science teaches wave speed as frequency times wavelength (NGSS HS-PS4-1), and the chocolate in the microwave is a classic classroom way to use it.

questions.question: Thomas Young let a thin beam of sunlight in through a small hole in a window and held a slip of card, about a thirtieth of an inch wide, edgewise in it, as he described in 1803. In the card's shadow, where light passing its two sides overlapped, he saw bright and dark bands. When he blocked the light passing one side, the bands vanished. What was happening in each dark band?
questions.answer: Light from the two sides met crest on trough and cancelled
choices: Light from the two sides met crest on trough and cancelled
Light from the two sides met crest on crest and added
Particles from the two sides collided and knocked each other away
The card's edges soaked up the light headed for those spots
questions.context: Where light from one side arrives half a wave behind light from the other, crest meets trough and the two cancel; where they arrive in step, they add into a bright band, and with one side blocked there is nothing left to cancel. Light added to light making darkness is what waves do, not a stream of particles, so the bands told against Isaac Newton's particle theory of light, though most scientists were won over only after Augustin Fresnel's and François Arago's work some fifteen years later. Light is now known to behave in some ways as a wave and in others as particles.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn constructive and destructive interference, and Young's experiment is the standard evidence that light behaves as a wave.

questions.question: Noise-cancelling headphones carry a tiny microphone that hears the steady drone of a jet engine. A circuit turns the drone's wave upside down and plays it from the headphone's speaker, so each crest of the drone meets a trough and the drone almost vanishes. Suppose the circuit fell behind and its wave reached the ear exactly half a wave late. What would the listener hear?
questions.answer: The drone, louder than with the speaker off
choices: The drone, louder than with the speaker off
The drone, cancelled just as well as before
The drone, cut to half its usual loudness
The drone, shifted up to a higher pitch
questions.context: A wave turned upside down and then delayed by half a wave is back in step with the drone, so crest meets crest and the two add: constructive interference instead of destructive. The timing must be right, which is why such headphones do best on low, steady sounds like engine drone and worse on high or sudden ones, whose short or changing waves are harder to match. Paul Lueg patented the idea in 1936, and working versions followed in the 1950s.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders apply constructive and destructive interference to devices, and noise-cancelling headphones are the curriculum's own example.

questions.question: The Titanic's sinking after it struck an iceberg in 1912 set inventors working on ways to find unseen things at sea by their echoes. By 1917 Paul Langevin, in France, was hunting submarines with pulses of ultrasound sent from quartz crystals. Suppose a ship's pulse comes back from an iceberg 4 seconds after it is sent, through sea water where sound travels about 1,500 metres a second. How far away is the iceberg?
choices: About 3,000 metres
About 6,000 metres
About 1,500 metres
About 750 metres
questions.context: In 4 seconds the pulse travels 6,000 metres, but that is the trip to the iceberg and back, so the iceberg lies half that distance away: sonar always halves the echo's round trip. Langevin's quartz crystals both sent the pulses and picked up their echoes, and in 1918 his set found submarines about 1,300 metres away. Echo sounders measure the depth of the sea the same way.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade physical science teaches how sonar uses reflected sound to measure distance, and the out-and-back trip is the step students most often miss.

questions.question: Ian Donald, a Glasgow professor of midwifery, took fibroid tumours and an ovarian cyst removed from patients to a boilermaker's works at Renfrew in 1955. There a machine found hidden cracks in steel by the echoes of ultrasound pulses, and he tried it on the specimens, with a large steak for comparison. Echoes come back from each boundary between one material and another, and a cyst is a thin-walled sac of fluid. What echoes did the cyst give?
questions.answer: Echoes from its near and far walls only
choices: Echoes from its near and far walls only
Echoes that faded steadily with depth
One strong echo from its near wall only
Echoes packed thickly from wall to wall
questions.context: Fluid has no boundaries inside it, so the pulse sends back nothing until it reaches the cyst's far wall, leaving a clear gap on the screen; a solid tumour, in Donald's words, gave echoes that weakened steadily the deeper the sound went. Later his scanner showed that a woman thought to be dying of stomach cancer had a huge, harmless cyst instead, which surgeons removed. Donald, John MacVicar and Tom Brown published their scans in 1958, among them the first published ultrasound image of an unborn baby.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn how ultrasound imaging uses reflection at boundaries between materials, and Donald's cyst is the founding case of reading an echo picture.

questions.question: Robert Watson-Watt and Arnold Wilkins showed near Daventry, in England, on 26 February 1935 that a bomber about eight miles off sends back enough of a radio beam to be picked up. Within a year their test set was finding aircraft over 100 miles away. Yet ships hunting a submarine under the sea rely on the pulses of sound that sonar sends out. Why can radar not find the submarine there?
questions.answer: Sea water soaks up radio waves within a short distance
choices: Sea water soaks up radio waves within a short distance
Steel hulls let radio waves pass straight through them
Sound travels through water faster than radio waves do
Radio waves need air to carry them along
questions.context: Sea water carries electric current, so it drains a radio wave's energy within a short way, about a quarter of a metre for some radio waves and less still for radar's microwaves, while sound crosses kilometres of sea. Radio waves are far faster than sound, need no air at all and reflect strongly off metal, which is how radar finds ships and surfaced submarines. Watson-Watt had first been asked whether radio could be made into a death ray, and Wilkins worked out that it would take impossible amounts of power.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade physical science (NGSS HS-PS4-5) covers radar and sonar as uses of reflected waves and how different materials absorb or pass waves.

questions.question: Glass fibres of the early 1960s lost light so fast that no signal could cross even a kilometre of them. Charles Kao, an engineer at a laboratory in Harlow, England, studied why, and in 1966 he and George Hockham argued that a glass fibre could carry light for kilometres after all. What did Kao find was robbing the fibres of most of their light?
questions.answer: Traces of other substances in the glass
choices: Traces of other substances in the glass
The glass itself, which scatters light by nature
Light escaping through the sides of the fibre
Light waves too long for so thin a thread
questions.context: Kao traced the loss to impurities such as iron and water in the glass, which could be removed, rather than to glass itself, and he pointed to pure fused silica; Corning made such a fibre in 1970, losing less light than his target. Light does not leak from the sides, because it strikes the edge of the fibre's core at a slant and is reflected back in completely, which is called total internal reflection. Kao shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics for the work.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade physical science teaches fibre optics as a use of light's behaviour at boundaries, and Kao's purer glass is the discovery that made fibre communication work.

questions.question: Christoph Buys Ballot loaded trumpeters onto an open railway car in 1845 and had a locomotive pull them along the line between Utrecht and Maarssen while they held one steady note. Listeners beside the track heard the note about a half-tone higher as the train came toward them and a half-tone lower as it went away, as Christian Doppler had predicted three years before. Why did the note sound higher as the train came on?
questions.answer: Each wave set out nearer, so the waves arrived bunched
choices: Each wave set out nearer, so the waves arrived bunched
The sound rode with the train, so it arrived faster
The note grew louder, and a louder note sounds higher
The rushing air pushed the trumpets' note higher
questions.context: Each crest leaves the trumpet a little nearer the listener than the one before, so the crests arrive closer together, more of them each second, and the note is higher; behind the train they are stretched apart, and it is lower. The trumpets' own note never changed, and the sound's speed is set by the air, not by the train. Police radar guns and Doppler weather radar read the same shift in the echoes of microwaves and radio waves to tell how fast a car, or the rain in a storm, moves toward or away from them.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade physics explains the Doppler effect by waves bunching ahead of a moving source, and Buys Ballot's trumpeters are its classic first test.

questions.question: Every long cable picks up electrical noise, so repeaters along the way strengthen the fading signal before passing it on. An analog cable carries a telephone call as a smooth wave shaped like the sound of the voice. A digital cable carries it as a code of on-and-off pulses, ones and zeros. Why does the digital call arrive clearer after many repeaters?
questions.answer: Each repeater sends out fresh pulses, dropping the noise
choices: Each repeater sends out fresh pulses, dropping the noise
Each repeater boosts the pulses more than the noise
The pulses travel faster than the smooth wave does
The pulses pick up no noise at all along the cable
questions.context: A pulse is either on or off, so a repeater only has to decide which, and noise too small to change that answer is dropped as it sends out a clean new pulse; an analog repeater amplifies the noise along with the voice, so the noise piles up stage after stage. Digital signals do pick up noise, but shrug it off up to that limit, and extra check bits catch many errors beyond it. Storing works the same way: each copy of a copy of a cassette tape grows hissier, while a digital recording can be copied again and again without loss.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade physical science (NGSS HS-PS4-2) asks students to explain why digital signals are more reliable to store and send than analog ones.
